segments.text: Welcome to your daily Robotics news digest for October 23, 2026.
We cover exciting developments, including new AI training methods, major roadmap shifts, and funding breakthroughs.
Tune in for the latest.
From Robotics & Automation News, "Google DeepMind uses Gemini 4 Argon to teach Apptronik’s Apollo humanoid new skills from video".

This report details how Gemini 4 Argon learned a physical task from video by analyzing spatial coordinates and calculating joint movements, resulting in the transfer of this learned behavior to the Apollo humanoid robot.

The process employed a Video-to-Sim-to-Real pipeline, which significantly reduced weeks of manual simulation work to just a few hours, aiming to decrease the manual engineering necessary for teaching robots new physical skills.
The system was evaluated on the Embodied Reasoning benchmark and achieved an eighty-seven percent score during testing.
This advancement suggests a pathway toward automating complex physical skill acquisition for robotic systems.
From Humanoid.guide, Brett Adcock says the Figure roadmap has completely changed.
This report details a significant alteration in the company's developmental trajectory over the last year, reflecting rapid progress.
The team size has also doubled in response to this advancement, according to Adcock.
The changes observed reflect rapid progress rather than any setbacks.

Adcock shared an internal staff meeting publicly to ensure alignment among employees regarding the company's mission, providing an overview of the organizational growth at the humanoid robotics developer.
This update provided a comprehensive look at the expansion of the humanoid robotics development organization.
This evolution signals significant acceleration in the field of humanoid robotics development.
From The Robot Report, "Dream Labs raises $90M and launches Dream API".
This story details the successful funding and launch of the Dream API by Dream Labs, a development that translates natural language and camera feeds into direct robot motor commands.
The Dream-1 model was developed to learn task execution by observing video, enabling zero-shot learning which allows robots to perform new tasks across different hardware without specific prior data.
The Dream API facilitates instant connection between any robot equipped with grippers and external applications for task performance.
Dream Labs also provides fine-tuning services and a robot playground for expanded developer engagement with the technology.
This development signals a significant step toward generalized robotic control via vision and language processing.
Further advancements in multimodal AI integration are anticipated across the robotics sector.

From TechCrunch - Robotics, a former OpenAI science lead launched Warp Science to automate wet labs with robots, an initiative focused on automating the synthesis and testing of compounds for drug discovery.
The company trains robots to perform these tasks, allowing them to synthesize and test promising chemical compounds identified by researchers.
Human chemists are involved in training these robots to execute various laboratory tasks, enabling continuous, twenty-four-seven robotic operation to accelerate the drug discovery process.
This effort is designed to reshore labor-intensive laboratory work currently outsourced and to mitigate geopolitical supply-chain risks associated with the work currently concentrated in China.
Warp Sciences has secured twenty-one million five hundred thousand dollars in funding and holds an eight hundred sixty-five million dollar valuation.
This development signals a trend toward integrating advanced artificial intelligence with physical robotics in scientific research.
From Robotics & Automation News, Infineon names winners of humanoid robotics startup challenge.
This report details the results of the 2026 Startup Challenge focused on humanoid robotics and physical AI, where the Italian startup AdapTronics was awarded the top position.
The competition assessed innovations in robotics and artificial intelligence, with AdapTronics winning for a technology that enables robots to handle objects without conventional grippers.
Other recognized winners included COSMOKE for tactile sensing and TECHiFAB for in-memory computing in motor control.
Infineon provided hardware, software, and artificial intelligence development tools to the competing teams throughout the process.
AdapTronics will now partner with Infineon to advance and scale its winning technology.
This development indicates continued focus on novel manipulation methods within the humanoid robotics sector.
From Robotics & Automation News, Generative Bionics to build European ‘physical AI data factory’ for humanoid robots.

This report details the creation of Europe's largest physical AI training facility for humanoid robots, which will utilize AMD computing infrastructure for real-world training and digital twin simulation.
The initial five thousand square meter facility is scheduled for construction in Italy and operational by late 2027, as part of a larger three site network.

This factory enables humanoid robots to generate physical data by executing tasks within replicated industrial environments, allowing models trained through simulations of various conditions to be validated on physical robots in a continuous real-to-sim-to-real cycle.
This initiative is designed to enhance European AI and industrial sovereignty through continental infrastructure development.
The project signals a significant step toward advancing physical-digital integration in the robotics sector.
From The Verge - Robots, "Just because Tesla’s Optimus is in production doesn’t mean it’s actually ready".
This report addresses the current status of humanoid robot manufacturing by Tesla and outlines the ongoing challenges in achieving full readiness.
Tesla is currently in the process of manufacturing humanoid robots like Optimus while simultaneously working to ensure they are useful, reliable, and durable.
CEO Elon Musk has acknowledged that significant work remains on the robot's hands, safety, reliability, durability, and the necessary artificial intelligence.
Musk anticipates that full delivery to outside companies will occur around the end of 2027, pending the resolution of these challenges.
To achieve this, Tesla needs to build a large fleet of robots to generate training data through self-play.
Experts suggest that solving the challenges of dexterity and reliability may take longer than Musk's timeline.
This indicates that the timeline for advanced humanoid deployment is contingent upon solving complex engineering hurdles in robotics and artificial intelligence.
From Robotics & Automation News, "70 Years On: Canton Fair Rewrites Robotics Sourcing – From Showroom Prototypes to Task-Ready Deployable Systems".
This report details a significant shift in robotics sourcing at the 140th Canton Fair, where international buyers are now prioritizing production-grade, deployable systems over mere prototypes.
International buyers are emphasizing systems ready for real-world application, driven by themes of innovation, the green transition, and smart manufacturing.

Exhibitors are demonstrating integrated technologies and hardware for diverse applications, including humanoid robots and autonomous inspection platforms, showcasing the entire robotics value chain from core components to end-to-end solutions.
Consequently, buyers are focusing on practical specifications such as uptime, maintenance requirements, and regulatory compliance rather than just demonstrations.
This trend indicates a maturation in the market toward commercially viable robotic deployments.
From Robotics & Automation News, "Opinion: Send the robot, not the person. What inspection robots are really for".
This report examines the role of inspection robots in industrial environments and their application in safety protocols.
Engineers utilize these robotic systems to gather data from hazardous locations, such as power substations, thereby minimizing direct human exposure to danger.
The methodology involves deploying autonomous robots to collect visual and sensor data from areas deemed too dangerous for personnel.
These robots are designed to collect evidence, yet the findings necessitate interpretation by human engineers who retain the capacity to contextualize the data and make final decisions.
Physical investigation remains necessary to fully understand complex site conditions, emphasizing that robotic data serves to augment, not entirely replace, human expertise in judgment and action.
The focus remains on outsourcing hazardous tasks while maintaining human oversight central to the operational process.
This trend indicates a continued focus on symbiotic human-machine systems in high-risk industrial applications.
From Robotics & Automation News, ETH scientists set to bring Terminator-style robots to life with lab-grown muscles.
This report details the creation of bioactuators by integrating living muscle tissue from mouse cells with three-dimensional printed hydrogel scaffolds, resulting in functional movement.

The methodology involved designing the muscle and scaffold as a single system using computer simulations to optimize movement, which yielded actuators exhibiting visible motion, including jumping and surface traversal.
This successful design underscores the significance of the interplay between living tissue and soft artificial structures.
Future work will focus on addressing the challenges of long-term nutrient supply and managing the variability inherent in living tissue.
This advancement points toward new possibilities in bio-integrated robotics and soft materials engineering.
From Robotics & Automation News, "Warehouse PPE and Hi Vis in the Age of Automation: Keeping People Safe Around the Machines".

This report examines the necessity of specific Personal Protective Equipment for personnel working in close proximity to automated machinery, establishing that essential items like high-visibility clothing, safety footwear, and gloves are standard practice based on risk assessments.
The implementation of a comprehensive Personal Protective Equipment strategy in automated warehouse environments requires adherence to established safety protocols.
Visibility is identified as crucial for ensuring that personnel are perceived by drivers and sensors, particularly in environments characterized by low light or cold storage conditions.
High-visibility clothing selection must be determined according to the specific role and risk zone, aligning with standards such as EN ISO 20471.
This strategy further mandates the inclusion of appropriate footwear, hand protection, and diligent garment maintenance for optimal safety outcomes.
The industry must continue to integrate these physical safety considerations into the design and operation of advanced automation systems.

From Robohub, Robot Talk Episode 167 – Automating construction, with Jan Petrš reports on novel robot designs for construction and architecture, highlighting research in tensegrity robotics and the combination of reconfigurable and soft robotics for these applications.
Jan Petrš, a roboticist and entrepreneur co-founding Déploya Robotics, discussed his work at the intersection of robotics and construction at EPFL.
The discussion detailed the development of deployable robotic systems specifically for automated façade installation, focusing on tensegrity robotics principles.
The research involves combining reconfigurable and soft robotics to create adaptable systems capable of handling complex architectural tasks efficiently.
This work addresses the integration of advanced robotics into the physical building environment.
The findings indicate a pathway toward more flexible and automated construction methodologies.
The ongoing development points toward increased autonomy in construction processes.
From Robotics & Automation News, 120ft emerges from stealth with €576,000 to build humanoid-powered microfactories.
This report details a Swedish robotics startup that secured angel funding to develop autonomous microfactories utilizing humanoid robots for local manufacturing.
The company is creating modular factories designed to enable consumer brands to assemble products locally in smaller batches, thereby circumventing lengthy international supply chains.
The system integrates humanoid robots, artificial intelligence, virtual simulation, and orchestration software to translate designs into digital assembly instructions.
Furthermore, 120ft has achieved a significant reduction in the time required for robot skill training, setting a goal for just seven minutes for full assembly by 2027.
The secured funding will be allocated to developing the factory infrastructure and software as the company progresses toward commercial production and future repair services.
This development indicates a focused trajectory for integrating advanced robotics into localized, on-demand manufacturing processes.
From Humanoid.guide, "Welcome, G1+!".
This report details the specifications and capabilities of the G1+ robot developed by Unitree Robotics, noting its high performance in navigation versus its limited manipulation skills.

The G1+ is a compact humanoid robot designed for research and education, achieving a perfect score of five out of five in navigation tasks while demonstrating a score of one out of five for basic manipulation tasks such as obstacle avoidance and sorting goods.
The robot measures one hundred thirty-four centimeters in height and weighs thirty-five kilograms, exhibiting locomotion abilities including running, jumping, and navigating stairs.
This version incorporates upgrades such as a stronger neck, dual cameras, and improved audio systems, and the platform is offered with software development kit support, focusing on movement studies.
This development indicates continued progress in integrating advanced locomotion systems into educational robotics platforms.
From Humanoid.guide, Neura unveils lighter 4NE1 Gen 4 as Munich RoboGym opens.
This report details the launch of a new humanoid robot model and associated training infrastructure at the Technical University of Munich.
The new 4NE1 Gen 4 robot features a slimmer physical design, upgraded hand mechanisms, and Smart Limbs designed to facilitate independent environmental responses and enhanced gripping precision.
Operation of the robot is managed by Neuron AI, a system that integrates vision, touch, force, and state data to direct its actions.
A new robot training center has been established at TUM, providing a facility for practical industrial task testing for various companies.
This center connects real-world tasks with data from robot movements, human demonstrations, and simulations to develop advanced robotic skills.
This development signals a progression in practical, data-driven humanoid robotics research.
From Humanoid.guide, "Welcome, 4NE1 Gen 3.5!".
This report details the specifications and development status of the 4NE1 Gen 3.5, a full-size humanoid robot designed for industrial applications.

The robot measures one hundred eighty centimeters tall and weighs eighty kilograms, incorporating fifty-five degrees of freedom and specialized sensors including a patented sensor skin and three-dimensional vision.

Development utilized NVIDIA Jetson Thor and NEURA's electric actuators to achieve capabilities such as obstacle avoidance, sorting goods, and product assembly, with navigation rated one out of five and manipulation rated two out of five.
Production is anticipated by the end of 2026 at a listed price of one hundred fifteen thousand US dollars.
This development signals further progress in the practical application of advanced robotics in manufacturing and logistics sectors.
From Humanoid.guide, "Welcome, RH56H1!".
This segment details the introduction and specifications of the RH56H1, a five-fingered robotic hand from Inspire Robotics.
The device measures 75 by 159 millimeters and weighs 0.48 kilograms, designed with a human hand format and an internal metal structure for humanoid robotics and prosthetics research.
Research indicates the hand has a low overall Hand Score of three out of ten, reflecting a modest dexterity and strength rating.
The hand is currently in production with a listed price of seven thousand US dollars.
This development contributes to ongoing research in advanced robotic manipulation and assistive technology applications.
From Humanoid.guide, "Welcome, Walker Tienkung!".
This report details the introduction of a humanoid robot designed for research and education that demonstrates advanced mobility skills.
The robot measures one hundred seventy centimeters in height and weighs fifty-five kilograms.
The platform possesses mobility skills including obstacle avoidance, one hundred meter running, and stair climbing, emphasizing movement over advanced manipulation.
It features forty-nine degrees of freedom and is constructed from aerospace-grade alloys with joint modules capable of three hundred newton meters of peak torque.

The system supports software environments such as Linux and ROS 2 for experimentation with humanoid movement and basic object handling, and the robot is commercially available for academic and research use at forty-one thousand United States dollars.
This development signals continued progress in the field of embodied artificial intelligence and robotic locomotion research.
From Humanoid.guide, "Welcome, Phoenix Gen 8!".
This report details the specifications and capabilities of the Phoenix Gen 8, an eighth-generation general-purpose humanoid robot.
The robot measures 170 centimeters tall and weighs 70 kilograms, featuring a humanlike upper body mounted on a wheeled base for stable positioning.
It possesses a lifting capacity of 25 kilograms, employing electric actuators and hydraulic hands equipped with fine tactile sensing.
The system has demonstrated abilities in obstacle avoidance, sorting goods, and product assembly, primarily focusing on physical manipulation tasks to collect data for the Carbon AI control system.
This device was released in December 2024 and is currently cataloged as a prototype with a listed price of one hundred fifty thousand United States dollars.
The advancement highlights a focus on physical task execution within humanoid robotics.
Further developments in physical manipulation capabilities are anticipated in the near future.
From Humanoid.guide, "Welcome, Dex!".
This segment details the specifications and current status of the industrial humanoid robot Dex developed by Richtech Robotics, noting its developmental stage.
Dex is an industrial humanoid designed for manufacturing, logistics, and warehouse environments, featuring two arms mounted on a mobile wheeled base or a stationary configuration.
The robot measures 137 centimeters in height and weighs 60 kilograms, employing an NVIDIA Jetson Thor for its computing platform and electric motors for locomotion.
The system supports functions such as obstacle avoidance, goods sorting, and product assembly utilizing modular end effectors.
Current assessments indicate a skill score of three out of ten and lower navigation and manipulation ratings, signifying ongoing industrial capability development.
Prototype trials are recommended prior to production deployment.
This development points toward continued refinement in the integration of advanced robotics for real-world industrial applications.
From RoboPapers, "Ep#112: SlipSense and Touch2Trace"
reports on advancements in tactile sensing for robotic applications, with key findings demonstrated through the SlipSense and Touch2Trace systems.

The SlipSense system employs a multimodal tactile sensor, the TacV5, integrating a piezoresistive array and an accelerometer to accurately detect object slipping with a detection time of 23.1 milliseconds and a ninety-six point seven percent Macro F1 score across one million frames.
The framework utilizes modality-specific encoders and cross-attention to fuse spatial pressure and vibration cues, indicating that these two modalities are complementary for slip detection.

Furthermore, the system exhibits zero-shot transfer to novel robotic platforms without retraining, and Touch2Trace shows that tactile feedback significantly enhances dexterous cable tracing compared to proprioception-only methods.
These developments suggest increased capability for robust, real-time tactile perception in robotic systems.

From Humanoid.guide, the Advanced Robotics Conference 2026 in Aachen focuses on Physical AI within humanoid robotics and seeks to address the challenges of deploying reliable and safe robotic systems in real-world industrial settings.

The event is scheduled to take place in Aachen on November 25 and 26, 2026, featuring nineteen speakers who will cover areas ranging from AI software and hardware to sensors, actuators, and industrial applications.

Discussions will concentrate on the integration of various technologies and the economic viability of advanced robotics, aiming to connect research, engineering, and industrial applications to create practical solutions.
This conference represents a convergence point for advancing the practical deployment of humanoid robotics technologies.
Industry observers should anticipate further developments in safe and economically viable robotic systems emerging from these discussions.
From TheSequence, "The Sequence Robotics - Issue #957: Generalist and the Rise of Promptable Robots"
details a method for enabling robots to perform complex physical interactions through conversational learning.
Large-scale physical pretraining creates a reusable foundation for robot behavior by utilizing short demonstrations to teach new tasks instead of requiring bespoke datasets.
Models across GEN-0, GEN-1, and GEN-1.5 have demonstrated nearly ninety-nine percent success on selected tasks via in-context physical prompting.
This research focuses on using conversational learning to allow robots to execute complex physical interactions.
The core investigation centers on whether these performance improvements translate into successful, long-horizon real-world deployments.
The findings suggest a pathway toward more generalist robotic systems capable of adapting to novel physical commands.
Further research will assess the viability of these results in complex operational environments.
And that's all the circuits for today!
Hope your day is as brilliantly engineered as Gemini 4.
Until tomorrow, keep those algorithms humming!
Bye for now.
